name: Arabic (Modern Standard)
summary: Modern Standard Arabic is a Semitic language written right to left in a cursive abjad: consonants and long vowels are letters, short vowels are optional marks, so reading depends on knowing the grammar. Its words are built by weaving consonantal roots into patterns, which gives derived verb forms I–X, broken plurals, verbal nouns and participles; nouns have two genders, three numbers (with a dual), three cases and a definite prefix, and agree in all four with adjectives — except that non-human plurals agree as feminine singular. There is no present 'to be' and no verb 'to have', numbers show gender polarity and govern the case and number of the noun, and negation, conditionals and 'that' each split into several words by tense or construction. The written standard sits above spoken dialects (diglossia), and everyday politeness is a system of fixed, gender-sensitive and often religious formulas.
sources: Wiktionary via kaikki.org (the course's reference data: forms, plurals, senses, etymologies)
W. Wright, A Grammar of the Arabic Language (3rd ed.)
K. C. Ryding, A Reference Grammar of Modern Standard Arabic (Cambridge, 2005)
W. Fischer, A Grammar of Classical Arabic (Yale, 3rd ed.)
H. Wehr, A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic (ed. J. M. Cowan)
K. Brustad, M. Al-Batal, A. Al-Tonsi, Al-Kitaab fii Taʿallum al-ʿArabiyya

phenomena.title: Right-to-left writing, numbers left-to-right
phenomena.what: Arabic is written and read from right to left, and books, pages, forms and tables start on the right. Numbers inside a line, and embedded words in left-to-right scripts, still run left to right (bidirectional text), which affects cursor movement, punctuation and mixed text.

examples.note: I am a student — read from the right
the digit ٣ (3) sits inside right-to-left text

model.other: language.json dir: "rtl"; §8 requires lang/dir on every foreign span; the RTL keyboard and script module are phase P4 (not built).

phenomena.gap: P4: on-screen keyboard and RTL input handling, a short page on bidirectional text (numbers, Latin inside Arabic).

phenomena.title: An abjad: consonants and long vowels only
phenomena.what: The 28 letters write consonants and the long vowels ā, ū, ī (with ا و ي); short vowels are optional marks. A normal text therefore leaves the reader to supply the vowels from grammar and context.

examples.note: one unvocalized spelling — كَتَبَ he wrote, كُتُبٌ books, كُتِبَ it was written

model.other: language.json vowelMarks: true; forms stored fully vocalized and the plain spelling derived with stripMarks (langcore); fn.overview peculiarities explain it.

phenomena.gap: script/letters.json (§4.9) and the letter stage (§5.5) do not exist yet; nothing trains reading the bare consonant skeleton.

phenomena.title: Cursive joining and positional letter shapes
phenomena.what: Letters are joined within a word and take up to four shapes: isolated, initial, medial and final. Six letters (ا د ذ ر ز و) never join the letter after them, which splits a word into pieces.

examples.note: rose — every letter stays unjoined because و ر د do not connect forward

model.other: Rendering is left to the font (Noto Naskh Arabic, §8); glyph_form and trace (§6.1) are listed but not implemented.

phenomena.gap: letters.json with positional forms and connecting behaviour; glyph_form and trace exercises; letter-stage gating (§5.5).

phenomena.title: The obligatory lam-alif ligature
phenomena.alsoNote: The obligatory لا ligature belongs to the Arabic script and is shared by every language written in it (Persian, Urdu …); other joining scripts do not have it.
phenomena.what: When ل is followed by ا (also أ إ آ) the two letters must be written as one ligature, لا. Learners who know the separate shapes often fail to recognise it.

examples.note: peace — the ligature inside a word

model.other: Produced automatically by the font; nothing teaches or tests it.

phenomena.gap: A letter-module entry and a glyph_form item for لا.

phenomena.title: Short-vowel marks (ḥarakāt) and sukūn
phenomena.what: fatḥa (a), kasra (i), ḍamma (u) and sukūn (no vowel) are small marks above or below the letter. They are written in the Qurʾān, children's books and dictionaries, and left out almost everywhere else; the course writes all of them and must later take them away step by step.
phenomena.record: Every stored form is fully vocalized (§4.5); the plain spelling is derived.

model.other: Every cell of every paradigm is vocalized; validate_lang.py rejects a form or lemma without marks; langcore.stripMarks / hasMarks; the tokenizer also reads unvocalized words (loose lookup).

phenomena.gap: The vowel-mark policy (fully → partially → unvocalized, §3.1, settings) is not implemented; no vowelize exercise.

phenomena.title: Šadda: the doubling mark
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian and Urdu write the same mark (tašdīd), mostly in Arabic loanwords. Hebrew dagesh once marked doubling but Modern Hebrew does not pronounce it; Japanese marks a doubled consonant with a small っ before it. Knowing gemination alone does not teach the mark.
phenomena.what: A doubled consonant is written once with a šadda above it. It is meaningful: it distinguishes verb forms and words, and it appears after the article before sun letters.

examples.note: he studied / he taught (form I / form II)
the flat — šadda for the sun letter and for the root

model.other: Stored in every form (U+0651 is one of the marks stripMarks removes).

phenomena.gap: No exercise contrasts single and doubled consonants (vowelize, spell).

phenomena.title: Tanwīn spelling and the extra alif of the accusative
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian and Urdu keep the written -an (ـاً) only in Arabic loan adverbs (فوراً، اتفاقاً); the Persian indefinite suffix -i is a different thing.
phenomena.what: Indefinite endings are written as doubled vowel marks (ـٌ ـً ـٍ). The accusative -an adds a written alif (كِتَابًا), except after ة and after ـاء, and the same -an ending makes many adverbs and formulas (شُكْرًا).

phenomena.title: Tāʾ marbūṭa (ة)
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew has the same alternation of the feminine ending, -a in isolation and -at- in the construct (ה → ת), but with two different letters; Persian and Urdu keep ة only in a few Arabic loanwords.
phenomena.what: The feminine ending ة looks like h with two dots; it is said -a in pause and -at- whenever something follows: a case ending, a possessive suffix, or a second noun in a construct. Before suffixes it is written ت.

phenomena.title: Alif maqṣūra (ى) and final -ā
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian and Urdu write a few Arabic loanwords with a final ی read ā (موسی، حتی).
phenomena.what: A final ā can be written ى (a dotless yāʾ). It turns into ي or ا when a suffix is added, and nouns in -an (مَقْهًى) keep the ى under their tanwīn.
phenomena.gap: No spelling rule page or spell exercise for ى ↔ ي/ا.

phenomena.title: Hamza and its seats
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian and Urdu write hamza on seats too, mainly in Arabic loanwords (مسئله، تأثیر), without the changes across a paradigm; Urdu ئ mostly marks a vowel sequence. Hebrew א has no seats.
phenomena.what: The glottal stop ء is a full consonant, but it is written on a seat (أ إ ؤ ئ) or alone (ء) by rules that depend on the surrounding vowels; the same root letter therefore changes its spelling across a paradigm.

model.other: Spelled in every form; roots write hamza as ء ("ء ك ل").

phenomena.gap: No rule page for the seats and no spell exercise with letter-level feedback on hamza (§6.1).

phenomena.title: Hamzat al-waṣl: the vanishing alif
phenomena.what: Some words begin with an alif whose vowel is heard only at the start of speech (the article al-, اِبْن, اِسْم, اِمْرَأَة, imperatives and forms VII–X). After a vowel it is silent and the words run together.

examples.note: at home — the a of al- disappears

model.other: The course writes the alif as اِ / اُ (teaching convention); validate_lang.py accepts ٱ or bare ا for it inside a sentence.

phenomena.gap: No explicit page or exercise; the transliteration of sentences (which shows the elision) is not generated.

phenomena.title: Sun and moon letters
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew ha- historically doubled the following consonant (dagesh) before any letter, and Modern Hebrew does not pronounce it; there is no assimilation of an l.
phenomena.what: Before the 14 sun letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن) the l of al- is not pronounced; the next consonant is doubled and carries šadda. Before the other 14 (moon) letters al- is said in full.

examples.note: the sun (sun letter) / the moon (moon letter)

phenomena.record: sunLetter (bool) on every noun and adjective, read from the DEF cell (written with šadda).
phenomena.gap: No sun/moon sorting drill and no transliteration of the DEF forms (translit is stored for the lemma only).

phenomena.title: Dagger alif and other historical spellings
phenomena.alsoNote: Urdu writes the same small alif in a few words (عیسیٰ، موسیٰ، اللّٰہ); Hebrew has historical defective spellings, a related but different idea.
phenomena.what: A few very frequent words have a long ā that is not written with a full alif but with a small superscript alif (or nothing in plain text): هٰذَا, ذٰلِكَ, لٰكِنْ, اللّٰه. مِائَة (hundred) has an alif that is not pronounced.

examples.note: hundred — the ا is silent (also spelled مِئَة)

model.other: U+0670 counts as a vowel mark in langcore.stripMarks.

phenomena.gap: Spelling variants (مِئَة) are not recorded; no pitfall page on these spellings.

phenomena.title: Arabic punctuation
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian and Urdu use the same turned marks ، ؛ ؟ (Urdu adds ۔ as its full stop); Hebrew uses the unturned marks. The long chains of clauses with وَ / فَ are a matter of Arabic prose style.
phenomena.what: The comma, semicolon and question mark are mirrored or turned (، ؛ ؟), and all marks follow the right-to-left direction. Traditional and much modern prose uses few full stops and links clauses with وَ 'and' and فَ 'so'.

model.other: The tokenizer splits any Unicode punctuation; bank sentences use ؟ and ،.

phenomena.gap: On-screen keyboard (P4) for ، ؟ ؛.

phenomena.title: Reading without vowels: homographs
phenomena.what: Without vowel marks many different words share one spelling; the reader decides by grammar and context. This is the central reading skill after the beginner stage.

model.other: langcore.lookup reads unvocalized words (loose) and returns every match; nothing uses this for teaching.

phenomena.gap: A graded reader with reduced marks, a 'which reading?' exercise built from the form index, and the vowel-mark policy setting.

phenomena.title: Learner transliteration (DIN 31635)
phenomena.alsoNote: DIN 31635 is a scheme for Arabic; scholarly transliterations of Persian and Urdu use similar conventions (macrons, ʿ, ʾ).
phenomena.what: Until the script is learned every word is shown with a scientific transliteration: macrons for long vowels, dots for emphatics (ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ ḥ), ʿ for ع and ʾ for hamza.
phenomena.record: translit on every lexeme: the pausal form without case or tanwīn ending (kitāb, šurṭī, muḥāmī, maqhā); adverbs and formulas in -an keep it, as it is part of the word (šukran, kaṯīran).

model.other: language.json romanization: din31635; principalParts shows the transliteration.

phenomena.gap: Transliteration exists only for lemmas (not forms or sentences); no transliterate exercise.

phenomena.title: Arabic-Indic digits
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian and Urdu use the extended Arabic-Indic digits ۰–۹, in which 4, 5 and 6 (and in Urdu 7) have other shapes; Hebrew uses 0–9 but shares the left-to-right numbers inside right-to-left text.
phenomena.what: The Arab East writes the Arabic-Indic digits ٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩; the Maghreb uses the digits 0–9, which come from the same Indian system. Inside right-to-left text a multi-digit number is still written with its highest digit on the left, so numbers are read left to right.

examples.note: read left to right inside right-to-left text

model.other: Shown in the numerals page; no lexeme or exercise uses the digits.

phenomena.gap: number_words / clock / date exercises (§6.5) with digits ↔ words.

phenomena.title: Emphatic (pharyngealized) consonants
phenomena.what: ص ض ط ظ are 'emphatic' (pharyngealized) versions of s, d, t, ð: the root of the tongue is pulled back towards the pharynx, and the vowels around them sound darker. They distinguish words from their plain partners.

model.other: Visible in the transliteration of every word (ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ); no word parameter of its own. Audio is phase P9.

phenomena.gap: A sounds page with minimal pairs, and audio (P9).

phenomena.title: Pharyngeal and glottal consonants: ع ح ء ه
phenomena.what: Four throat consonants are kept apart: ʿ (ع, a voiced pharyngeal [ʕ], a squeeze in the throat), ḥ (ح, a voiceless pharyngeal [ħ], a strong breathy h), h (ه, glottal [h]) and the glottal stop ʾ (ء, [ʔ]). Each distinguishes words and can stand anywhere in the word.

examples.note: he asked — a glottal stop inside the word

model.other: Visible in the transliteration of every word (ʿ ḥ h ʾ); no word parameter of its own. Overview mentions ع ح ق as new sounds; audio P9.

phenomena.gap: Sounds page with minimal pairs; audio (P9).

phenomena.title: Uvular and velar fricatives: ق خ غ
phenomena.what: ق is a voiceless uvular stop [q], made at the uvula, further back than k; خ is a voiceless uvular (or velar) fricative [χ ~ x]; غ is its voiced partner [ʁ ~ ɣ], a sound between a gargled r and a voiced fricative. Each distinguishes words from k, h and r.

model.other: Visible in the transliteration of every word (q ḫ ġ); no word parameter of its own.

phenomena.gap: Sounds page with minimal pairs and bridges to de/ru/el; audio (P9).

phenomena.title: Interdental consonants: ث ذ ظ
phenomena.what: ث is the voiceless interdental fricative [θ], ذ the voiced one [ð], and ظ an emphatic [ðˤ]: the tongue tip is between the teeth. Most spoken dialects replace them with t/s, d/z (and ḍ/ẓ), so a speaker's dialect can show in their Standard pronunciation — another diglossia trap.
phenomena.gap: Sounds page using the Greek bridge; audio (P9).

phenomena.title: Phonemic vowel length
phenomena.what: Short and long vowels are different sounds and different spellings (a mark versus a letter); length alone separates words and verb forms.

examples.note: he wrote / he corresponded with (form I / form III)

phenomena.gap: No listening or spelling drill on length.

phenomena.title: Phonemic consonant length (gemination)
phenomena.what: A doubled consonant is held longer and changes the word; in pattern morphology doubling is a meaningful element (form II, the faʿʿāl profession pattern).
phenomena.gap: No contrastive drill; audio (P9).

phenomena.title: Predictable stress by syllable weight
phenomena.what: Stress is not written and not lexical: it falls on the last syllable if it is superheavy (long vowel + consonant, or two consonants), otherwise on the penult if it is heavy (long vowel, or vowel + consonant), otherwise on the antepenult. It never distinguishes two words.
phenomena.gap: A short rule page; audio (P9).

phenomena.title: Pausal forms (waqf)
phenomena.alsoNote: Biblical Hebrew has pausal forms; Modern Hebrew does not.
phenomena.what: At the end of a phrase final short vowels and tanwīn are not pronounced, -an becomes -ā and ة is said -ah. Everyday reading aloud uses pause forms almost everywhere, so the written case endings are often not heard.
phenomena.gap: Pause forms are only mentioned; no transliteration or audio of them.

phenomena.title: Helping vowels before a consonant cluster
phenomena.what: A word ending in a consonant takes a short vowel before al- or another hamzat al-waṣl so that two consonants do not meet: مِنْ → مِنَ, عَنْ → عَنِ, هَلْ → هَلِ.

model.other: The variant is an extra cell (ADP;ALT) or in alts — paradigm data, not a word parameter: ar:min and ar:an have ADP;ALT cells; ar:hal, ar:aw, ar:am, ar:man, ar:liman have alts.

phenomena.title: Consonantal roots
phenomena.what: Most words are built on a root of three (sometimes four) consonants that carries a field of meaning. Knowing the root links dozens of words and is how dictionaries are ordered.

examples.text: ك ت ب → كَتَبَ، كِتَاب، مَكْتَب، كَاتِب
ط ب خ → طَبَخَ، مَطْبَخ، طَبَّاخ

phenomena.record: root on every noun, adjective, verb, adverb, number and preposition: the radicals separated by spaces ("ك ت ب"), or {none: why} for a loanword, a phrase or a particle.

model.other: Every native word carries its root (the days of the week, the kin terms, مَدِينَة قَرْيَة بَلَد سُوق …); langcore.principalParts shows it.

phenomena.gap: root_family / root_pattern exercises are not implemented (only a quiz).

phenomena.title: Weak roots (hollow, defective, assimilated, doubled, hamzated)
phenomena.what: When و or ي is a root letter it turns into a long vowel or disappears, a doubled root contracts under šadda, and a hamza changes its seat. The class of the root predicts the shape of the whole paradigm.

examples.note: hollow root ق و د: he drove, I drove, he drives
defective root م ش ي: he walked, he walks
assimilated root و ص ل: the و drops in the present
doubled root ح ب ب: the pair separates before a consonant ending

phenomena.record: rootClass on every verb: sound | hollow | defective | assimilated | doubled | hamzated (one or more).
phenomena.gap: rootClass is stated for verbs only (nouns show the root); fn.past (cr.01) has a table of hollow, defective and doubled verbs in the past, but no page lists the full paradigm pattern of every class.

phenomena.title: Patterns (awzān) for nouns and adjectives
phenomena.what: The vowels and extra letters around the root make a pattern with a meaning of its own: mafʿal (place), mifʿāl (tool), fāʿil (doer), faʿʿāl (trade), mafʿūl (thing done), fuʿla and others. Patterns are named with the model root ف ع ل.
phenomena.record: pattern on every noun and adjective, in ف ع ل letters with the traditional measure (بَاب فَعَل، مَطَار مَفْعَل، مُسْتَشْفًى مُسْتَفْعَل), or {none: why} (loanword, phrase); the plural’s pattern in each plurals item.
phenomena.gap: root_pattern exercise (root × pattern → word, word → root + pattern).

phenomena.title: Derived verb forms I–X
phenomena.what: From one root up to ten verb forms are built, each with typical meanings (II causative/intensive, III doing with someone, V reflexive of II, VII passive-like, VIII reflexive, X asking for or considering). Each form has a fixed present, participle and maṣdar pattern.

examples.note: to know (I) → to teach (II) → to learn (V) → to inquire (X)
to buy — form VIII of ش ر ي

phenomena.record: verbForm: I … X (or none for laysa and other defective verbs).

model.other: Every verb states verbForm; principalParts shows it.

phenomena.gap: The analyze exercise (form → verb form) and a table of the ten forms with their present/participle/maṣdar patterns.

phenomena.title: Perfect and imperfect: suffix and prefix conjugations
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew: past = suffix conjugation, future = prefix conjugation (its present is a participle). Amharic: perfective with suffixes, imperfective with prefixes.
phenomena.what: Every verb has two finite stems: the perfect with person endings (past, completed) and the imperfect with person prefixes (present, and the base of the moods and the future).

model.other: fn.past (cr.01) teaches the suffix conjugation with tables of sound and weak verbs; the bank (c01_04) has Tense variants PST ↔ PRS and PRS ↔ FUT.

phenomena.title: The imperfect stem vowel of form I
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew pa'al has the same o / a choice in the future (יִכְתֹּב / יִלְמַד), more predictable than in Arabic (a near gutturals and in many statives).
phenomena.what: For form I verbs the vowel of the present stem (a, i or u) cannot be predicted from the past; it is learned with each verb (dictionaries give it).
phenomena.record: present: the 3rd person singular imperfect (يَفْعَلُ) on every verb, shown in the facade section of the word card.
phenomena.gap: langcore.principalParts still lists only root and verb form for an Arabic verb (the present appears in the facade section); no stem-vowel drill.

phenomena.title: Moods of the imperfect: indicative, subjunctive, jussive
phenomena.alsoNote: The أَنْ-subjunctive matches the subjunctive of Romance languages, German or Greek only in part; the jussive (also the past after لَمْ) has no counterpart there. Amharic has a jussive ("let him …"); Biblical Hebrew had one, Modern Hebrew does not.
phenomena.what: The imperfect has three moods shown by the ending: indicative -u, subjunctive -a (after أَنْ، لَنْ، لِـ 'in order to'), jussive with no vowel (after لَمْ, prohibitive لَا, and لِـ of command). An energetic mood exists in formal style.

model.other: لَمْ + jussive in fn.past (cr.01), لَنْ + subjunctive in fn.future (cr.03); the jussive and subjunctive cells come from Wiktionary’s tables (formsAlt for doubled-verb variants).

phenomena.gap: JUS and SBJV cells are stored only on the verbs of cr.01–cr.03 (paradigmCells.VERB does not require them, so older verbs lack them); no moods function of its own; the prohibitive لَا + jussive is not linked to fn.imperative.

phenomena.title: Verb agreement: person, number (with dual) and gender
phenomena.what: The verb shows person, number and gender in the 2nd and 3rd persons, and has dual forms: 13 forms per tense. A pronoun subject is usually dropped.
phenomena.gap: The dual (3 persons × 2 tenses) is not in paradigmCells.VERB and no verb stores it; dual pronouns أَنْتُمَا / هُمَا are not in the lexicon.

phenomena.title: The imperative and its helping alif
phenomena.alsoNote: The Hebrew imperative is also cut from the future (תִּכְתֹּב → כְּתֹב), without a helping alif.
phenomena.what: The imperative is cut from the jussive 'you' form; a helping alif (اِ / اُ) is added when it starts with two consonants. Four forms by addressee (plus a dual).

examples.note: go! — to a man, a woman, men, women

phenomena.title: Suppletive and defective verbs
phenomena.what: A few verbs borrow missing forms from another root: 'come!' is تَعَالَ, not a form of جَاءَ. لَيْسَ has only perfect-shaped forms with present meaning.

examples.note: I am not tired — perfect-shaped, present meaning

model.other: A separate lexeme with class imp / defective and the same concept (تَعَالَ beside جَاءَ; لَيْسَ); their present, maṣdar and participles are stated as none with the reason.

phenomena.title: The internal passive
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew pu'al and huf'al are internal u–a passives of pi'el and hif'il (the passive of pa'al is nif'al, a prefix form).
phenomena.what: The passive is made by changing the vowels, not with an auxiliary: u–i in the perfect, u–a in the imperfect. Unvocalized it looks exactly like the active.
phenomena.gap: Passive cells (V;PASS;…), a function and transforms.

phenomena.title: Future with سَـ / سَوْفَ
phenomena.what: The future is the imperfect with the prefix سَـ or the separate particle سَوْفَ before it. It is negated with لَنْ + subjunctive, not with لَا.

examples.note: I will go (more distant or emphatic)

model.other: Lexemes سَـ (prefix), سَوْفَ and لَنْ (cr.03, role words); Tense variants PRS ↔ FUT and Polarity variants with لَنْ in the bank.

phenomena.title: كَانَ + imperfect: past habit and progress
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew says a past habit with הָיָה + participle; Amharic puts a finite imperfective before ነበር. Elsewhere the meaning is familiar, the two finite agreeing verbs are not.
phenomena.what: كَانَ followed by an imperfect verb gives the past continuous or habitual ('was doing, used to do'); both verbs agree with the subject.

examples.note: he was eating / he used to eat

model.other: fn.past.ongoing (cr.02, status periphrastic): كَانَ + present for the background and the habit; Aspect, Number, Mood and Polarity variants in the bank.

phenomena.title: The verbal noun (maṣdar)
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew has a verbal noun for every binyan (כְּתִיבָה، דִּבּוּר، הַפְעָלָה) next to its infinitive; the pa'al one is fairly regular, the Arabic form I one is not.
phenomena.what: Each verb has a verbal noun that does the work of an infinitive or a gerund. For form I it is unpredictable and must be learned; for forms II–X it follows the form.
phenomena.record: masdar (strings) on every verb, or none for لَيْسَ and تَعَالَ; a maṣdar that belongs to one meaning is in meaningForms (عَادَ “visit”: عِيَادَة).
phenomena.gap: The maṣdar is shown in the facade section, not as a principal part; no exercise.

phenomena.title: No infinitive: the 3rd-person past as citation form
phenomena.what: Arabic has no infinitive. Dictionaries cite a verb by its 'he did' form; 'to do' in a sentence is أَنْ + subjunctive or the maṣdar. Dictionaries are ordered by root.

examples.note: lit. 'he ate' — the dictionary form of 'to eat'

model.other: language.json citationCells.VERB = V;PST;3;SG;MASC (validated).

phenomena.title: Active and passive participles
phenomena.what: Every verb form has an active and a passive participle by pattern (fāʿil / mafʿūl, mu-…-i- / mu-…-a- for derived forms). They serve as adjectives, nouns of agent and object, and as a present-progressive in many contexts.
phenomena.record: participles on every verb: [{form, kind: active | passive}] — the passive only for verbs with an object.

model.other: Many participles are lexemes of their own (طَالِب، سَائِق، مُعَلِّم) with no link to their verb.

phenomena.gap: No derivation link from the verb to participle lexemes (طَالِب، سَائِق، مُعَلِّم); no exercise.

phenomena.title: Two genders, with covert feminines
phenomena.what: Every noun is masculine or feminine; there is no neuter. Most feminines end in ة, but some are feminine without it (sun, earth, house دَار, paired body parts, كَأْس), and nouns for women are feminine whatever their form.
phenomena.record: gender: MASC | FEM (both for a few nouns).

model.other: gender is declared at the top level for every noun (نَاس and أَجْدَاد are masculine plurals).

phenomena.title: The dual
phenomena.what: Exactly two is a grammatical number of its own on nouns, adjectives, pronouns, demonstratives and verbs: -āni (nominative) / -ayni (accusative and genitive). With a noun the dual alone says 'two'.
phenomena.record: dual on every noun (the nominative dual, also of phrases: مَكْتَبَا بَرِيدٍ), or {none: why} for mass nouns, names and plural-only words; DU cells in the paradigms.

model.other: 110 of 248 nouns have DU cells; paradigmCells.NOUN does not require them.

phenomena.gap: DU cells are not required for every countable noun; the dual pronouns (أَنْتُمَا، هُمَا) and demonstratives (هٰذَانِ، هَاتَانِ) and the dual verb cells are missing.

phenomena.title: Sound masculine plural -ūna / -īna
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew -im is the counterpart (and its construct -ei drops the m like -ūna drops the -na), but it serves all masculine nouns and has no case forms.
phenomena.what: Mostly for male human participles and adjectives: -ūna in the nominative, -īna otherwise; the final -na drops in a construct and before a suffix.
phenomena.record: Inside the plurals list of nouns and adjectives: kind soundMasc (the parameter is named after ar.morph.plural.broken / .multiple).
phenomena.gap: The construct form without -na (مُعَلِّمُو) is not stored (no CONST cells for these nouns).

phenomena.title: Sound feminine plural -āt
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew -ot is the counterpart, without case forms.
phenomena.what: For female persons, many nouns in ة, loanwords and maṣdars of derived forms: -ātun, with -ātin in both accusative and genitive (no -an).
phenomena.record: Inside the plurals list: kind soundFem (the parameter is named after ar.morph.plural.broken).

phenomena.title: Broken (internal) plurals
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew changes stem vowels together with a plural suffix (מֶלֶךְ → מְלָכִים) but has no true broken plurals; Amharic keeps a few learned Ge'ez broken plurals (ኮከብ → ከዋክብት); Persian and Urdu use Arabic broken plurals of Arabic loanwords (کتب، اخبار).
phenomena.what: Most nouns form the plural by a new pattern of the root (about thirty common patterns). The plural is not predictable from the singular with certainty and is learned with the word.
phenomena.record: plurals on every noun: [{form, kind, pattern, declension, note, senses}], or {none: why} for mass nouns, names and words used in the singular only.

model.other: The paradigm’s PL cells hold the main plural; the plurals list states the kind, pattern and declension and adds the other plurals, each tied to its meanings.

phenomena.gap: An exercise grouping plurals by pattern; the plural drills do not read the plurals list yet.

phenomena.title: Several plurals for one noun, sometimes by meaning
phenomena.alsoNote: German has a few plurals by meaning (Worte / Wörter); the paucity / multitude pair has no counterpart.
phenomena.what: A noun can have two or more plurals: free variants, a plural of paucity (3–10) next to a plural of multitude, or different plurals for different meanings.
phenomena.record: plurals: several items, each with senses (the profile sense ids): بُيُوت / أَبْيَات / بُيُوتَات, عُمَّال / عَوَامِل, كِبَار / كُبَرَاء, أَخْوَال / خِيلَان.

model.other: formsAlt still holds some variant plurals for the paradigm; the per-meaning plurals are in plurals and the word card shows them with each meaning.

phenomena.gap: Principal parts show only the paradigm’s plural; drills do not use the per-sense plurals yet.

phenomena.title: Collective nouns and unit nouns
phenomena.what: Many fruits, vegetables, animals and materials have a collective (the kind, the mass) and a unit noun in ة (one piece, a singulative), which has its own dual and plural for counting.
phenomena.record: class collective + unit (the unit noun) on every collective.

model.other: principalParts shows collective, unit and counted plural.

phenomena.gap: Collective agreement (fem. sg. or masc.) is not recorded.

phenomena.title: Diptotes (no tanwīn, genitive in -a)
phenomena.what: Some nouns and adjectives (many broken plural patterns, أَفْعَل adjectives, many proper names, feminines in -āʾ) never take tanwīn and use -a for the genitive when indefinite. With al- or in a construct they decline normally.

examples.note: schools – in schools – in the schools

phenomena.record: declension on every noun and adjective: the singular’s type (of the head noun in a phrase) — triptote | diptote | defective | invariable | dual — and a declension in every plurals item.

model.other: Month names are diptotes, phrases included: كَانُونُ الثَّانِي — the head كَانُون takes no tanwīn and -a in the genitive; مَايُو، كُوسَا are invariable.

phenomena.gap: A rule page with the diptote patterns; a contrast drill.

phenomena.title: Three cases (iʿrāb)
phenomena.what: Nominative -u, accusative -a, genitive -i, written as short vowel marks. Nouns are subject/predicate (nominative), object and adverbial (accusative), after prepositions and as second noun of a construct (genitive). Duals and sound plurals have long-vowel endings instead.

examples.note: the student read the book (nom. … acc.)

phenomena.record: kind on every preposition: ḥarf (a true preposition) | ẓarf (an accusative noun used as one) | phrase.

phenomena.title: Definiteness: al- and tanwīn
phenomena.what: 'The' is the prefix al- written on the word; 'a' is the tanwīn ending. Definiteness is also given by a possessive suffix or a definite second noun of a construct, and is an agreement feature of the adjective.

examples.note: I like coffee — generic statements use al-, as in Greek

model.other: det.def and det.indef are marked absent with the reason in fd.01.

phenomena.title: The construct state (iḍāfa)
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew has the same construct state (סְמִיכוּת: בֵּית סֵפֶר), next to the particle שֶׁל.
phenomena.what: 'X of Y' is two nouns side by side: the first loses al- and tanwīn and takes the case of its place, the second is genitive and decides definiteness for both. It replaces most compounds and genitive phrases.

examples.note: a door of a house / the door of the house

model.other: CONST cells exist only for kin, quant and number words; the dual of a phrase is stated in its construct form (مَكْتَبَا بَرِيدٍ); multiword lexemes (مَكْتَب بَرِيد) store construct forms. No construct parameter: the forms are paradigm data.

phenomena.gap: CONST cells for all nouns (dual بَيْتَا, sound plural مُعَلِّمُو); a dedicated construct function and transform.

phenomena.title: The five nouns (أَب، أَخ، حَم، فُو، ذُو)
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew אָב and אָח keep a trace: -i- before suffixes (אָבִיו، אָחִיו).
phenomena.what: A small group shows case by a long vowel before a genitive or a suffix: -ū, -ā, -ī.

model.other: Irregular construct and possessive cells in the kin paradigm (paradigm data, not a parameter); NOUN.kin has only nominative construct/possessive cells (and GEN 1sg).

phenomena.gap: ACC and GEN construct and possessive cells for أَب / أَخ (أَبَا، أَبِي; أَخَاكَ، أَخِيكَ).

phenomena.title: Attached pronouns on nouns, verbs and prepositions
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew attaches the same pronouns to nouns, verbs (formal style) and prepositions (לִי، אִתּוֹ). Persian has possessive and object clitics, Amharic possessive and object suffixes, but not on prepositions in the same way.
phenomena.what: Possessors, objects and prepositional objects are suffixes: -ī/-ya my, -ka/-ki your, -hu his, -hā her … On a verb 'me' is -nī, not -ī.
phenomena.record: suffix on every personal pronoun (ـكَ، ـهُ، ـهَا …); the suffixed forms as cells (POSS;PSS…, ADP;person, PART;person).
phenomena.gap: Object suffixes on verbs (V;…;OBJ cells or a morph_build exercise); POSS cells exist mostly for kin nouns and in the nominative.

phenomena.title: Attached prefix words: وَ فَ بِـ لِـ كَـ سَـ أَ and al-
phenomena.what: One-letter words are written together with the next word, and up to three can stack. لِـ + al- loses the alif: لِلْـ.
phenomena.record: prefix (true / false) on every preposition, coordinating conjunction and particle; the host keeps its own forms.

model.other: Tokenizer strips up to two prefixes (langcore.lookup); prefix lexemes: وَ فَ بِ لِ أَ سَ (سَـ since cr.03); bank tokens with parts.

phenomena.gap: كَـ is not a lexeme; لِـ + al- (لِلْـ, لِلّٰهِ) is not handled by the tokenizer (the rest لْبَيْتِ matches no form) and no bank sentence uses it.

phenomena.title: Gender in 'you' and 'they'
phenomena.alsoNote: Spanish has gender in "you" and "they" only in the plural (vosotros / vosotras, ellos / ellas); a gendered singular "you" is new there.
phenomena.what: Second-person pronouns, verb forms and suffixes differ for a man and a woman (and for groups of women); 3rd-person plural too. Speaking to someone requires knowing their gender.

examples.note: you (to a man / to a woman)

phenomena.record: person on every personal pronoun (person, number, gender).

model.other: Separate lexemes per gender; transform variants Addressee / Gender.

phenomena.title: Adjective agreement in four features
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew repeats the article on the adjective and agrees in gender and number (no case); Romanian and Albanian agree in case but mark definiteness on the adjective differently.
phenomena.what: The adjective follows the noun and agrees in gender, number, case and definiteness (al- is repeated on the adjective). Human plurals take plural adjectives, non-human plurals feminine singular.

phenomena.title: The elative أَفْعَل (comparative and superlative)
phenomena.what: One pattern serves as comparative (with مِنْ 'than') and superlative (with al- or before a genitive). The comparative does not inflect for gender; the definite superlative has a feminine fuʿlā.
phenomena.record: elative on every adjective (أَكْبَر), or {none: why} with the way it is compared (أَشَدُّ بَيَاضًا، أَكْثَرُ تَعَبًا).
phenomena.gap: The feminine superlative (فُعْلَى) and the plural (أَفَاعِل / أَفْعَلُونَ) are not stored.

phenomena.title: Colour and defect adjectives أَفْعَل / فَعْلَاء / فُعْل
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew has patterns of its own for colours (אָדֹם، יָרֹק) and for bodily defects (עִוֵּר، אִלֵּם), but not one shared pattern with a feminine and plural of its own.
phenomena.what: Basic colours (and bodily defects) have a pattern of their own: masculine أَفْعَل, feminine فَعْلَاء, plural فُعْل. They look like elatives but cannot be compared directly.

phenomena.title: Relational adjectives (nisba) in -iyy
phenomena.what: The suffix -iyy (fem. -iyya) makes adjectives of origin, material or relation from nouns, including colours from things; the same form serves as a noun for a person ('an Egyptian').
phenomena.record: derivedFrom on every adjective: the base noun of a nisba (بُنِّيّ ← بُنّ), the verb of a participle (بَارِد ← بَرَدَ), or none for a basic adjective.

model.other: The nouns in -iyy (شُرْطِيّ) show the measure فُعْلِيّ.

phenomena.gap: A short rule page; useful for nationalities later.

phenomena.title: Diminutive pattern fuʿayl
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew and Amharic form diminutives by suffixes or by repetition (כְּלַבְלַב), not by an inserted -ay-.
phenomena.what: A pattern with -ay- makes diminutives; it is mostly lexicalised and frequent in names.
phenomena.gap: Later: a pattern note; low priority.

phenomena.title: Gender polarity of 3–10
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew 3–10 have the same polarity (שָׁלֹשׁ בָּנוֹת / שְׁלֹשָׁה בָּנִים).
phenomena.what: The numbers 3–10 take the opposite gender of the counted noun's singular: with a masculine noun the number has ة, with a feminine noun it has none.
phenomena.record: polarity (bool) on every number; MASC/FEM cells of the number.

phenomena.title: Number and case of the counted noun
phenomena.what: After 3–10 the noun is a genitive plural; after 11–99 an accusative singular; after 100 and 1000 a genitive singular. 1 and 2 are said by the noun alone (singular, dual).
phenomena.record: countedNoun on every number (agrees / dual alone / GEN;PL / ACC;SG / GEN;SG).
phenomena.gap: number_words exercise (§6.5) that builds number + noun from digits.

phenomena.title: Compound numbers: 11–19 and units before tens
phenomena.what: 11–19 are fixed two-part compounds ending in -a; from 21 the unit comes first and is joined to the ten with وَ 'and' (one-and-twenty).
phenomena.gap: 21–99 compounds are not in the lexicon or the bank; number_words exercise.

phenomena.title: Ordinal numbers and the clock
phenomena.alsoNote: Russian names the hour in progress with an ordinal (пятый час), a partial parallel.
phenomena.what: Ordinals use the fāʿil pattern of the root (except 'first'); the hour is said with a feminine ordinal: 'the fifth hour'.
phenomena.record: ordinal on every number (أَوَّل، ثَالِث، حَادِيَ عَشَرَ، الْعِشْرُونَ).

model.other: Ordinal lexemes أَوَّل … عَاشِر and أَخِير (cr.04) with full ADJ paradigms; time.oclock stays absent (fd.15).

phenomena.gap: Ordinals above ten (الْحَادِيَ عَشَرَ …) are not lexemes; the clock and date exercises of §6.5 are not implemented (the lesson uses bank sentences, transforms and a quiz).

phenomena.title: Nominal sentences: no 'to be' in the present
phenomena.what: A subject and a predicate simply stand side by side, both in the nominative. كَانَ appears in the past and future and puts its predicate in the accusative.

model.other: Bank frames fr.be.person, fr.be.where.

phenomena.title: Article decides phrase or sentence
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew works the same way (הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל / הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל).
phenomena.what: With al- on both noun and adjective it is a phrase; with al- only on the noun it is a complete verbless sentence. The same holds for demonstratives.

examples.note: this student / this is a student

phenomena.title: VSO and SVO with agreement asymmetry
phenomena.what: Both verb-first and subject-first orders are normal. A verb before a noun subject stays singular (showing only gender); a verb after it agrees fully.

model.other: Explained in the 'ask yourself' procedure of fn.present; build_sentence accepts alts.

phenomena.gap: A WordOrder transform variant and a contrast exercise (§6.4) for the agreement.

phenomena.title: Non-human plurals agree as feminine singular
phenomena.what: Plurals of things, animals and ideas take feminine singular adjectives, verbs and pronouns; only plurals of people take plural agreement.
phenomena.record: human (bool) on every noun.
phenomena.gap: The agree generator (§6.3) is not implemented.

phenomena.title: كَانَ and لَيْسَ put the predicate in the accusative
phenomena.alsoNote: Russian and Ukrainian put the predicate of быть / стать in the instrumental, a close parallel with another case.
phenomena.what: The 'sisters of kāna' (كَانَ, لَيْسَ, أَصْبَحَ, مَا زَالَ …) keep the subject nominative and make the predicate accusative.
phenomena.record: governs: predicate ACC (on كَانَ, لَيْسَ).

phenomena.title: إِنَّ and its sisters: accusative subject
phenomena.what: إِنَّ, أَنَّ, لٰكِنَّ, لِأَنَّ, كَأَنَّ, لَعَلَّ must be followed by a noun in the accusative or a pronoun suffix; the predicate stays nominative.
phenomena.record: governs on every conjunction: ACC+suffix (أَنَّ، لِأَنَّ، لٰكِنَّ) | SBJV | PST | clause.
phenomena.gap: إِنَّ itself, كَأَنَّ and لَعَلَّ are not in the lexicon.

phenomena.title: Negators chosen by sentence type and tense
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew also chooses the negator by sentence type (לֹא، אֵין، אַל), but not by tense with a change of mood.
phenomena.what: لَا + present, لَمْ + jussive for the past, لَنْ + subjunctive for the future, لَيْسَ for verbless sentences, مَا + past in classical and dialectal style, and لَا + jussive for 'don't!'.

model.other: لَمْ (cr.01) and لَنْ (cr.03) are role words with Polarity variants in the bank.

phenomena.gap: Jussive and subjunctive cells exist only on the verbs of cr.01–cr.03; no contrast exercise (§6.4) over the negators لَا / لَمْ / لَنْ / لَيْسَ / مَا.

phenomena.title: Questions: هَلْ, أَ, أَمْ and بَلَى
phenomena.alsoNote: Only the initial question particle is shared with Irish, Welsh or Estonian; French si / German doch match بَلَى, and Finnish vai / tai match أَمْ / أَوْ.
phenomena.what: A yes/no question puts هَلْ (or the prefix أَ) before the unchanged statement. In a choice question 'or' is أَمْ, not أَوْ. 'Yes' that contradicts a negative question is a word of its own, بَلَى.

examples.note: do you want tea or coffee?
don't you like tea? — yes, I do!

phenomena.title: An adjective after a construct: case shows which noun it describes
phenomena.what: Nothing may come between the two nouns of an iḍāfa, so every adjective follows the whole construct; its case and gender show which noun it belongs to.

examples.note: the big door of the house (nominative, with بَاب)
the door of the big house (genitive, with الْبَيْت)

phenomena.gap: A point in a construct function; bank sentences with variants.

phenomena.title: The adverbial accusative of time, place and manner
phenomena.what: Time and manner are often said with a bare accusative noun, without a preposition; most adverbs are frozen accusatives in -an.

model.other: derivedFrom on adverbs names the base word (كَثِيرًا ← كَثِير، الْيَوْمَ ← يَوْم).

phenomena.title: The circumstantial accusative (ḥāl)
phenomena.alsoNote: Russian depictives in the instrumental (пришёл усталым) are a partial parallel.
phenomena.what: An indefinite accusative describes the state of the subject or object during the action.
phenomena.gap: A function after the past (core grammar).

phenomena.title: Relative clauses: الَّذِي only after definite heads, with a resumptive pronoun
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew and Persian also repeat the head as a pronoun, but use one relativizer (שֶׁ، که) after any head.
phenomena.what: The relative pronoun agrees with a definite head (الَّذِي، الَّتِي، الَّذِينَ …); after an indefinite head there is none. The clause repeats the head as a pronoun.
phenomena.gap: Relative pronoun lexemes (with dual and plural forms) and the cr.06 function.

phenomena.title: Three 'if's: إِذَا, إِنْ, لَوْ
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew separates a real אִם from an unreal לוּ / אִלּוּ — two of the three.
phenomena.what: إِذَا is a likely or expected condition, إِنْ an open possibility (with the jussive or past), لَوْ an unreal condition (with لَـ in the result). The past tense is used after إِذَا even for the future.

examples.note: if I were rich, I would travel

model.other: Only إِذَا is a lexeme.

phenomena.gap: إِنْ and لَوْ lexemes and the cr.05 function.

phenomena.title: 'There is': fronted place, هُنَاكَ, يُوجَدُ
phenomena.alsoNote: Russian also fronts the place before an indefinite subject; Hebrew uses יֵשׁ.
phenomena.what: An indefinite subject does not start a sentence: the place phrase comes first, or the sentence opens with هُنَاكَ or يُوجَدُ.

examples.note: there is a book in the house

phenomena.gap: يُوجَدُ is not in the lexicon; 'there is' is only a sense of هُنَاكَ.

phenomena.title: Possession without 'to have'
phenomena.what: 'To have' is a preposition with a suffix: عِنْدَ (have, own), لِـ (belongs to, kinship), مَعَ (have on me). The possessed thing is the grammatical subject; past with كَانَ, negation with لَيْسَ.

phenomena.title: Verbs with fixed prepositions or a direct object
phenomena.what: Many verbs take a fixed preposition for their object, others a direct object; which one is a property of the verb (and sometimes of its meaning) and must be learned per verb.

examples.note: to wait for the bus (direct object)

phenomena.record: governs on every verb: [{case, prep, what, senses}], per meaning (ذَهَبَ إِلَى، اِنْتَظَرَ + ACC، عَادَ الْمَرِيضَ).
phenomena.gap: The prepositions of adjectives (قَرِيبٌ مِنْ، بَعِيدٌ عَنْ) are not a parameter; no collocation exercise.

phenomena.title: The vocative يَا
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian (ای, literary) and Irish (a) have a vocative particle, without the loss of the article.
phenomena.what: People are called with يَا before the name or title; a definite address noun loses al-.

model.other: Appears only in profile senses (يَا عَمِّي، يَا أُخْتِي).

phenomena.gap: A يَا lexeme and a short pragmatics page.

phenomena.title: Paternal and maternal relatives have different words
phenomena.what: Uncles and aunts are named by the side of the family: عَمّ / عَمَّة on the father's side, خَال / خَالَة on the mother's. There is no single word for cousin, nephew or niece: they are 'son of my paternal uncle' and so on.

examples.note: my cousin (son of my father's brother)

model.other: Separate lexemes per side, told apart by contrasts (axis “side of the family”); family.cousin, family.nephew, family.niece are marked absent with the eight descriptive phrases.

phenomena.gap: A sense_split exercise (§6.2) for the side of the family; the descriptive phrases are not lexemes.

phenomena.title: Formulas that change with the listener (and the speaker)
phenomena.alsoNote: Spanish adjectives in formulas agree with the speaker or listener (encantado / encantada), but its singular "you" has no gender.
phenomena.what: Every polite formula that contains 'you' has a form for a man, a woman and a group; formulas that describe the speaker (آسِف 'sorry') agree with the speaker.

examples.text: تُصْبِحُ عَلَى خَيْرٍ / تُصْبِحِينَ عَلَى خَيْرٍ
examples.translit: tuṣbiḥu ʿalā ḫayrin / tuṣbiḥīna ʿalā ḫayrin
examples.note: good night (to a man / to a woman)
sorry (said by a man / a woman)

phenomena.record: addressee on every formula (INTJ): MASC | FEM | PL | any.

model.other: One lexeme per addressee; transform variant Addressee.

phenomena.gap: The forms of one formula are not linked to each other; the plural forms (كَيْفَ حَالُكُمْ) are not lexemes.

phenomena.title: No polite 'you' (no T/V distinction)
phenomena.what: There is no polite pronoun of address: أَنْتَ / أَنْتِ is said to everyone. Politeness comes from formulas (مِنْ فَضْلِكَ), titles (أُسْتَاذ، سَيِّد، دُكْتُور) and kin terms. A plural of respect exists only in high style.

examples.note: please, sir (to a teacher or professional)

phenomena.gap: Titles (أُسْتَاذ، سَيِّد، سَيِّدَة) are not lexemes; a register / dialogue_turn exercise (§6.5).

phenomena.title: Greetings with fixed answers
phenomena.alsoNote: Set replies to greetings also exist in Turkish (hoş geldiniz – hoş bulduk), Swahili (shikamoo – marahaba) and others, but not the Arabic echo-and-outdo pairs.
phenomena.what: Many greetings require a set reply that echoes and outdoes them.

examples.note: peace be upon you → and upon you be peace
morning of goodness → morning of light

phenomena.record: response on every formula (INTJ): the fixed answer, or none.

model.other: The answers are lexemes with role and no concept.

phenomena.gap: The answer is text, not a link to the answer lexeme; dialogue_turn exercise.

phenomena.title: Religious formulas in everyday speech
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian, Urdu and Turkish use the same Arabic formulas (inşallah, maşallah …), as do many languages of Muslim communities (Somali, Hausa, Swahili, Malay, Indonesian, Azerbaijani, Uzbek …); Hebrew has its own (בְּעֶזְרַת הַשֵּׁם، בָּרוּךְ הַשֵּׁם).
phenomena.what: Formulas naming God are used by Muslims and Christians alike as ordinary politeness: for the future, for good news, before starting, when praising.

examples.note: God willing — said of anything in the future
praise be to God — 'fine, thank God'
what God has willed — admiration, against envy

model.other: Only الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ is a lexeme.

phenomena.gap: Lexemes for إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ، مَا شَاءَ اللّٰهُ، بِسْمِ اللّٰهِ with usage notes; bridges to Turkish inşallah, maşallah.

phenomena.title: Diglossia: Standard Arabic and the dialects
phenomena.what: Modern Standard Arabic is written and used formally; everyone speaks a regional dialect at home, with different words, pronouns and verb forms. The learner must know that everyday speech will differ.
phenomena.record: variants: [{lemma, region}] on lexemes; register on senses.

model.other: Dialect words appear only as profile synonyms with region.

phenomena.gap: The variants field (§4.5) is unused in ar; dialect layers are planned for later.

phenomena.title: Regional variation inside the Standard: month names
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew month names come from the same Babylonian set (תַּמּוּז، אָב، אֱלוּל), but in a different calendar.
phenomena.what: The Levant and Iraq use old Syriac-Babylonian month names, Egypt, the Gulf and the Maghreb Latin-based ones; both are standard and often written together.

model.other: One lexeme per region (the month names), told apart by contrasts on the axis “region”.

phenomena.gap: A region field so the app can pick the learner's set and quiz the pairs.

phenomena.title: Loanwords in and out: bridges for the learner
phenomena.alsoNote: Which loans a learner already knows is computed from the bridges, not from the tags. Hebrew also fits loans into its patterns (לְסַמֵּס).
phenomena.what: Arabic has old loans from Greek, Persian and Aramaic and newer ones from Italian, French and English, usually fitted into Arabic patterns (often with a broken plural: فِيلْم → أَفْلَام). It has lent words to many languages — Persian, Turkish, Urdu, Swahili, Malay, Spanish and, through them, much of Europe (sugar, coffee, algebra); the app shows the bridges that matter for each learner's languages.

model.other: Etymologies are in profiles; bridges.json (§4.10) does not exist yet.

phenomena.gap: bridges.json with cognates/loans and the cognate_bridge / etymology_link exercises (P6).

phenomena.title: False friends
phenomena.alsoNote: Which pairs are false friends is computed from the bridges for each learner, not from the tags.
phenomena.what: Words that travelled between Arabic and other languages often changed meaning on the way, so a familiar-looking word can mislead. Which pairs are false friends depends on the learner's languages; the app derives them from the bridges (§4.10).

examples.note: mother's sister — Turkish hala = father's sister

phenomena.gap: bridges.json entries with kind falseFriend.

phenomena.title: The week and the calendar
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew also starts the week on Sunday, with its own lunisolar calendar; Persian, Urdu, Turkish and other languages of Muslim communities know the Hijri months and Friday prayer.
phenomena.what: The week starts on Sunday; Friday (الْجُمُعَة, 'the gathering') is the day of congregational prayer and, with Saturday, the weekend in many Arab states. Religious life follows the lunar Hijri calendar (رَمَضَان …), which moves about eleven days a year against the solar calendar.

examples.note: the month of fasting (9th Hijri month)

model.other: Day names are lexemes; Hijri months are absent.

phenomena.gap: Hijri month names and a culture note.

phenomena.title: Days of the week named by numbers
phenomena.what: Sunday to Thursday are named after the numbers one to five (the root of each name is the number); Friday is 'the gathering' and Saturday 'the sabbath'.

model.other: The day names carry the roots of the numbers (ء ح د، ث ن ي، ث ل ث، ر ب ع، خ م س) and of ج م ع، س ب ت.

phenomena.gap: A root_family item linking the days to the numbers.

phenomena.title: Names: kunya (أَبُو / أُمُّ) and nasab (اِبْن)
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew uses בֶּן / בַּת in religious names (a nasab), but has no kunya.
phenomena.what: Parents are respectfully called 'father/mother of' their (eldest) child; traditional names chain 'son of'.

model.other: Senses s3 of أَب and أُمّ, s2 of اِبْن.

phenomena.gap: A culture note on names; bank sentences.

phenomena.title: Kin terms as polite address
phenomena.alsoNote: Swahili (mama, kaka, dada) and many other languages address strangers with kin terms too; having two kinds of uncle does not imply it (Swedish does not).
phenomena.what: Strangers are addressed as relatives: an older man 'uncle', an older woman 'auntie', a peer 'brother' or 'sister'.
phenomena.gap: A pragmatics note and dialogue exercises (§6.5).

phenomena.title: Concepts said with a construct instead of a compound
phenomena.what: New concepts made of two nouns are mostly said as an iḍāfa (construct) or noun + adjective, not as one-word compounds; the whole phrase inflects as a unit (the first noun takes the case, the second the article).

examples.note: a bedroom / the bedroom (lit. room of sleep)

model.other: Multiword lexemes with full forms; the tokenizer matches multi-word spans first.

phenomena.title: Proverbs, Qurʾānic phrases and rhymed sayings
phenomena.what: Proverbs (أَمْثَال) and fixed classical phrases are frequent in speech and writing; many are rhymed or parallel.

examples.text: الْوَقْتُ كَالسَّيْفِ، إِنْ لَمْ تَقْطَعْهُ قَطَعَكَ
examples.translit: al-waqtu ka-s-sayfi, ʾin lam taqṭaʿhu qaṭaʿaka
examples.note: time is like a sword: if you do not cut it, it cuts you

model.other: Profiles have phrases; idiom_meaning (§6.2) is not implemented.

phenomena.gap: The idiom_meaning exercise.

phenomena.title: Polysemy and homonymy inside roots
phenomena.alsoNote: The principle of meanings grouped in one root is familiar to Hebrew and Amharic speakers; the particular pairs are Arabic's own (see polysemy).
phenomena.what: One word often covers concepts that many languages keep apart (house / verse, grandfather / luck, maternal uncle / mole), sometimes with a different plural per meaning; distinct roots also coincide in spelling.

examples.note: house; verse of a poem (plural أَبْيَات)

phenomena.record: profile.senses: every meaning a concept or “of” another; per-meaning plurals (plurals.senses) and per-meaning forms (meaningForms: يَمِين “oath” is feminine, اللَّيْلَةَ tonight, عِيَادَة).

model.other: The word card shows every meaning with its own forms.

phenomena.gap: sense_pick exercise.

phenomena.title: كُلّ and بَعْض are nouns in construct
phenomena.what: 'All', 'every' and 'some' are nouns followed by a genitive: كُلّ + definite plural = all, كُلّ + indefinite singular = every.

phenomena.title: No capital letters
phenomena.what: The script has no upper and lower case: names, sentence beginnings and titles are written with the same letters as every other word, so a name is recognised from context (and from words like يَا or السَّيِّد before it).

examples.note: Muhammad travelled to Cairo — the two names look like any other word

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: el, en, de, ru, tr, es, fr, fi, hu, sw, lg, vi.

phenomena.title: One script for the language
phenomena.what: Arabic is written in one script, the Arabic alphabet, in all countries and registers (calligraphic styles such as naskh and ruqʿa are styles of the same letters). Informal chat sometimes uses Latin letters with digits for missing sounds (3 = ع, 7 = ح), but this has no official status.

examples.note: Arabic — the same letters in print and handwriting
informal Latin chat spelling, 3 standing for ع

phenomena.gap: The overview can say that there is one script (and that chat Latin exists); handwriting styles (ruqʿa) are not taught.

phenomena.title: Spaces between words — with small words attached
phenomena.alsoNote: Hebrew attaches the same kind of one-letter words (ו ה ב ל כ מ ש) and pronoun suffixes; Persian attaches far fewer.
phenomena.what: Words are separated by spaces. One-letter words (وَ فَ بِـ لِـ كَـ سَـ) and the article are written together with the next word, and pronoun suffixes with the word before, so one written word can be a whole phrase; the letter shapes also mark word ends (final forms).

examples.note: and with the pen — four words, one written unit
I wrote it — verb + subject + object in one word

phenomena.gap: Segmenting a written word into its clitics is shown on words but not practised as a reading skill.

phenomena.title: No lexical tone
phenomena.what: Pitch never changes a word's meaning: a word keeps its meaning whether said high, low, rising or falling, and the script has nothing to mark pitch. Pitch carries intonation only — a question can be marked by rising intonation as well as by هَلْ — and stress follows from syllable weight.

examples.note: he wrote. / he wrote? — the same word; only the sentence melody differs
did he write? — the question shown by a particle, not by pitch on the word

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: zh, vi, lg, ja (pitch accent).

phenomena.title: Syllable structure: no initial clusters, at most two final consonants
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian has the same CV(C)(C) syllable with a consonant at every syllable start; Turkish also bans initial clusters but allows syllables that begin with a vowel.
phenomena.what: Syllables are CV, CVC and CVV; at the end of a word in pause also CVVC and CVCC, and CVVC before a doubled consonant (دَابَّة). A syllable never begins with two consonants: words that would start with a cluster take a helping vowel (hamzat al-waṣl), and inside a word no more than two consonants meet. Final two-consonant clusters (كَلْب kalb) are frequent in pause.

examples.note: name — a helping vowel instead of an initial cluster sm-

phenomena.gap: Pause forms and helping vowels are described; no exercise trains syllable shapes or initial vowel insertion.

phenomena.title: Voiced and voiceless consonants — with gaps
phenomena.what: Voicing distinguishes words in stops and fricatives: t/d, s/z, θ/ð, ḫ/ġ, ṭ/ḍ. The system has gaps: b has no voiceless partner p, f has no voiced partner v, k has no voiced partner g (ج is [dʒ] in most Standard pronunciation), and ḥ, ʿ form a voiceless/voiced pharyngeal pair. Loanwords with p or v are written with ب / ف.

examples.note: bus — p of the loanword said and written as b

phenomena.gap: Minimal pairs are not drilled; the missing p / v / g is not stated.

phenomena.title: No ejective or implosive consonants
phenomena.what: No consonant is ejective or implosive. The 'heavy' consonants ص ض ط ظ are pharyngealized (tongue root pulled back), not glottalized, and the glottal stop ء is a consonant of its own, not a feature added to others.

examples.note: he repented / it was good — plain t vs pharyngealized ṭ

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: vi.

phenomena.title: No click consonants
phenomena.what: All consonants are made with air from the lungs; there are no clicks. Sounds made far back in the mouth or throat (ق ع ح) are ordinary pulmonic consonants.

examples.note: heart — q is a uvular stop, not a click

phenomena.gap: say it in the overview (fd.00) for learners whose languages have clicks.

phenomena.title: No retroflex consonants
phenomena.what: t, d, s, n, l are made with the tongue tip at the teeth or the ridge behind them, never curled back; the second, 'heavy' series ṭ ḍ ṣ ẓ is distinguished by a retracted tongue root (pharyngealization), not by retroflexion.

examples.note: figs / clay — dental t vs emphatic ṭ

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: hi, mr, zh.

phenomena.title: Aspiration does not distinguish words
phenomena.what: Whether t or k is said with a puff of breath never changes a word (it is lightly aspirated automatically). The contrasts that do matter in this place are voicing (t/d) and emphasis (t/ṭ).

examples.note: figs / clay / religion — t, ṭ and d are the distinctions, not aspiration

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: hi, mr, ko, zh, vi.

phenomena.title: Three vowel qualities, no front rounded vowels
phenomena.what: The vowel system has three qualities, a, i, u, each short or long, plus the diphthongs ay and aw. There are no front rounded vowels (ü, ö) and no separate e or o; emphatic and guttural consonants only colour a towards [ɑ] and i, u slightly.

examples.note: house / houses — a, u, ū and the diphthong ay

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: fr, de, tr, fi, hu, zh, and the five-vowel systems of el, es, ja, sw.

phenomena.title: No nasal vowels
phenomena.what: Vowels are never nasal by themselves: an n after a vowel is always pronounced as a full consonant, as in the tanwīn ending -un, -an, -in.

examples.note: a book — u followed by a full n

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: fr, hi.

phenomena.title: No vowel harmony
phenomena.what: Suffixes do not change their vowels to match the stem: -nā, -ka, -kum, -tu keep their vowels after any stem. The one small assimilation is the pronoun -hu / -hum, which becomes -hi / -him after i, ī or ay.

examples.note: our book / your book — the suffix vowels never adapt
his book / in his book — the only assimilation: -hu → -hi after i

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: tr, fi, hu.

phenomena.title: No final devoicing
phenomena.what: Voiced consonants stay voiced at the end of a word and before voiceless ones: in pause وَلَد keeps its d and كَلْب its b.

examples.note: a boy — the final d stays voiced in pause

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: ru, de, tr.

phenomena.title: Two liquids: r and l
phenomena.what: r (ر, a tapped or trilled tongue-tip r) and l (ل) are separate consonants that distinguish words. l is 'dark' only in the name اللّٰه (after a or u); r is often darkened next to a and u.
phenomena.gap: No minimal-pair practice for r / l.

phenomena.title: No palatalized consonants
phenomena.what: Consonants have no soft (palatalized) and hard series, and k, t, s, d keep their sound before i and y; consonant changes in Arabic come from emphasis and from the assimilation of al-, not from a following front vowel.

examples.note: book — k and t unchanged before i

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: ru.

phenomena.title: Unstressed vowels keep their quality
phenomena.what: In the Standard every vowel keeps its quality and length whether stressed or not: each a, i, u is said as it is written. (Spoken dialects drop many short unstressed vowels, another difference between the two registers.)

examples.note: school — the stressed and the unstressed a sound the same

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: ru, en.

phenomena.title: No initial consonant mutation
phenomena.what: A word's first consonant never changes because of the word before it or its grammatical role; the sound changes Arabic has are the assimilation of the l of al- to sun letters and the vowel changes of patterns.

examples.note: house / in my house / the house — b never changes

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: fi.

phenomena.title: Fusional inflection: one ending, several meanings
phenomena.what: One ending usually carries several grammatical meanings at once and cannot be split into a part per meaning: in كَتَبْتُ the -tu means 1st person + singular (and, with the stem, perfect); -āni means dual + nominative; -īna masculine + plural + accusative/genitive. With root-and-pattern stems this makes Arabic a fusional language with large paradigms.

examples.note: I wrote / you (m.) wrote / you (f.) wrote — one ending for person, number and gender
two teachers (nom.) / (acc.–gen.) — dual and case in one ending

phenomena.title: Mostly suffixes, with prefixes on the imperfect and the article
phenomena.what: Inflection is mostly at the end of the word: case, number and gender endings, possessive and object pronouns, and the person endings of the perfect. Grammar is also at the start of the word in the person prefixes of the imperfect (يَـ تَـ أَ نَـ) and the article al-, and inside it in the root patterns.

examples.note: I wrote it — stem + subject suffix + object suffix
they write — the imperfect has a prefix and a suffix

phenomena.title: Reduplicated roots and repeated words
phenomena.what: Reduplication is not a grammatical inflection, but it builds words: four-consonant verbs repeat a two-consonant syllable (the faʿfaʿa type), mostly for repeated sounds and movements; and a repeated word expresses distribution or gradual progress.

examples.note: they came in one by one

phenomena.gap: Reduplicated quadriliteral roots and distributive repetition are not mentioned.

phenomena.title: No noun incorporation
phenomena.what: An object noun is never built into the verb: it stays a separate word, or becomes an attached pronoun suffix, which is a pronoun and not a noun stem.

examples.note: he eats the bread / he eats it

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: iu.

phenomena.title: One 'we': no inclusive / exclusive
phenomena.what: نَحْنُ 'we' (and the verb forms and suffix -nā) covers both 'we including you' and 'we without you'; context tells which.

examples.note: we are going to the market — with or without the listener

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: mr, zh, vi.

phenomena.title: No numeral classifiers
phenomena.what: A numeral combines directly with the noun, without a counting word; instead the number decides the noun's case and number (genitive plural after 3–10, accusative singular after 11–99). A mass or collective noun is counted through its unit noun in ة.

examples.note: three books — numeral + noun, no classifier
three apples — via the unit noun تُفَّاحَة

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: zh, vi, ja, ko.

phenomena.title: One kind of possession
phenomena.what: All nouns are possessed the same way: body parts, relatives and objects take the same suffixes and the same construct, with no separate 'inalienable' marking.

examples.note: my hand / my brother / my car — the same suffix

phenomena.gap: say it in the overview (fd.00) for learners whose languages have alienable / inalienable possession.

phenomena.title: No progressive form
phenomena.what: There is no special form for an action in progress: the imperfect يَكْتُبُ means both 'he writes' and 'he is writing'. An active participle (أَنَا ذَاهِبٌ 'I am going') or, in the past, كَانَ + imperfect can bring out the ongoing sense.

examples.note: he writes / is writing a letter

model.other: fn.present says that one form covers “I eat” and “I am eating”; fn.past.ongoing (cr.02) shows كَانَ + present for “was doing”; notes for the reference languages compare it (D18).

phenomena.title: No separate perfect tense
phenomena.what: There is no perfect ('has done') distinct from the past: the perfect stem covers both. The particle قَدْ before it stresses completion or present relevance ('has already'), and لَمْ … بَعْدُ says 'has not yet'.

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: en, de, es, el.

phenomena.gap: بَعْدُ “yet” (لَمْ … بَعْدُ) is not a lexeme; قَدْ is a role word (cr.01) without a concept of its own.

phenomena.title: No dedicated wish form
phenomena.what: Wishes and blessings have no verb form of their own: the past (perfect) is used with wish meaning, لَا + past for a negative wish, and لِـ + jussive for 'let him …'.

examples.note: may God have mercy on him — a past form as a wish

phenomena.gap: Wish formulas are not explained as perfect forms with wish meaning.

phenomena.title: No grammatical evidentiality
phenomena.what: The verb does not show how the speaker knows something (seen, heard, inferred); the source is given by words when needed.

examples.note: it is said that he travelled

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: tr, ja, ko, iu.

phenomena.gap: Not yet said for fa, nor against the reportative conditional / subjunctive of fr, de and fi.

phenomena.title: No mirative
phenomena.what: Surprise is not a verb category; it is shown by intonation, interjections and the exclamative pattern مَا أَفْعَلَ + accusative ('how … !').

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: tr, ko.

phenomena.gap: The exclamative pattern (مَا أَجْمَلَ …!) is not in the course.

phenomena.title: No antipassive
phenomena.what: No verb form demotes the object; when the object does not matter it is simply left out.

examples.note: he is eating — no object, the verb unchanged

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: iu.

phenomena.title: No applicative
phenomena.what: No affix turns a beneficiary or an instrument into the verb's object; they stay prepositional phrases with لِـ or بِـ. (Some derived forms change what the object is, e.g. form III كَاتَبَ 'write to someone'.)

examples.note: I wrote him a letter — the beneficiary with لِـ

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: sw, lg, iu.

phenomena.title: No particle verbs
phenomena.what: No separable prefixes or adverbial particles change a verb's meaning; new meanings come from the root and the derived forms I–X. A fixed preposition belongs to the object and stays before it.

examples.note: come back / bring back — a derived form, not a particle

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: en, de, ru, hu.

phenomena.title: Few noun + 'do' verbs
phenomena.what: New verbs are made from roots and patterns, not as noun + 'do / make'. A few periphrases with قَامَ بِـ 'carry out' + verbal noun are frequent in news style.

examples.note: he paid a visit — news style

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: hi, fa, tr, ja, ko.

phenomena.title: No verb–object compounds
phenomena.what: A verb and its object never fuse into one word; the activity is named with a verbal noun in a construct.

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: zh.

phenomena.title: No converbs: ḥāl, conjunctions and وَ instead
phenomena.what: There is no adverbial verb form ('having done', 'while doing'). Simultaneous action is a ḥāl (an accusative participle, or وَ + clause), a sequence is joined with فَ or ثُمَّ, and time clauses use conjunctions such as عِنْدَمَا and بَعْدَ أَنْ.

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: tr, ja, ko, iu, mr (fn.connectors).

phenomena.gap: The gerunds and adverbial participles of el, ru, es, en, fr, hi, fi and hu are not compared yet; the ḥāl (ar.syn.hal), the nearest Arabic means, comes later.

phenomena.title: No honorific verb forms
phenomena.what: Verbs do not change for the rank of the subject or the listener; respect is shown by titles and formulas, and in high style by a plural of respect.

examples.note: please (come in / go ahead), sir — an ordinary imperative with a title

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: ja, ko.

phenomena.title: Demonstratives before the noun
phenomena.what: هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ 'this' and ذٰلِكَ / تِلْكَ 'that' agree in gender and number and stand before a noun with al-. After a construct or a noun with a suffix they follow it. Without al- on the noun the same words make a sentence ('this is a …').
phenomena.gap: Order after constructs and suffixed nouns is not practised.

phenomena.title: Question words at the start
phenomena.what: Question words (مَنْ who, مَا / مَاذَا what, أَيْنَ where, مَتَى when, كَيْفَ how, لِمَاذَا why, كَمْ how many) open the clause; the rest keeps statement order. مَا asks before a noun or in a verbless clause, مَاذَا before a verb; كَمْ takes an accusative singular noun.

examples.note: how many books do you have?

phenomena.gap: مَا / مَاذَا and كَمْ + accusative singular are not contrasted in exercises.

phenomena.title: Negative concord: 'nobody' needs a negated verb
phenomena.what: 'Nobody', 'nothing' and 'never' are normally a negated verb + أَحَد 'anyone', شَيْء 'anything' or أَبَدًا 'ever'; these words are not negative by themselves. (With the negation of absence لَا + accusative, لَا أَحَدَ 'nobody' can also open a sentence on its own.)
phenomena.gap: The negation lesson teaches لَا … شَيْئًا and لَا … أَبَدًا; أَحَد 'anyone' is not a lexeme.

phenomena.title: Subject-prominent, with fronted topics
phenomena.what: Sentences are built around a grammatical subject that the verb or the predicate agrees with. A topic can be put first and picked up by a pronoun in the rest of the sentence, but it then becomes the grammatical subject (mubtadaʾ) of a nominal sentence and is nominative.

examples.note: the house — its door is big
the girl came in — the verb agrees with its subject

phenomena.gap: The topic + resumptive pronoun sentence is not taught.

phenomena.title: Adverbials after verb and object
phenomena.what: Prepositional phrases and adverbs of place and time normally follow the verb and its object; they can be fronted for emphasis or to set the scene.

examples.note: I read the book in the library yesterday

phenomena.title: No verb-second rule
phenomena.what: The verb is not bound to second position: it can open the clause (VSO) or follow the subject (SVO), main and subordinate clauses have the same orders, and a fronted adverb does not move the verb.

examples.note: he said that Ahmad went yesterday — the same order in a subordinate clause

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: de.

phenomena.title: No serial verbs
phenomena.what: Two verbs are not simply strung together for one event: a second action is joined with وَ, فَ or ثُمَّ, put in a ḥāl, or made a subordinate verb with لِـ / أَنْ. Only verbs of beginning (أَخَذَ، بَدَأَ) take a following imperfect directly.

examples.note: he took the book and read it

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: zh, vi.

phenomena.title: No switch-reference marking
phenomena.what: Verbs do not mark whether the next clause has the same subject; the person, number and gender agreement of each verb shows who acts.

examples.note: he came in and (he) sat down
he came in and she sat down — only agreement shows the change

phenomena.gap: say it in the overview (fd.00) for learners whose languages have switch-reference.

phenomena.title: No grammatical speech levels
phenomena.what: There are no polite verb endings or speech levels; the register difference that matters is Standard vs dialect (diglossia), and politeness lies in formulas, titles and indirect requests.

examples.note: please — 'if you allow', an ordinary verb form

model.other: Comparison notes on fn.overview (D18) say it for the reference languages that have it: ja, ko, vi.

phenomena.title: Brother and sister without age
phenomena.what: أَخ 'brother' and أُخْت 'sister' do not say who is older; age is added with the elative adjective when it matters.
phenomena.gap: أَخ / أُخْت are lexemes (fd.06); elder / younger is not taught.

phenomena.title: Two verbs 'to know'
phenomena.what: عَرَفَ (يَعْرِفُ) is 'know' by acquaintance — a person, a place, a language — and is also used for facts in everyday Standard; عَلِمَ (يَعْلَمُ) is 'know (that)', knowledge of a fact, in formal style. In the negative, لَا أَدْرِي 'I don't know' is also common.

examples.note: I know that he is here

phenomena.gap: Neither عَرَفَ nor عَلِمَ is a lexeme yet.

phenomena.title: One verb 'to wear'
phenomena.what: لَبِسَ (يَلْبَسُ) is said of any clothing, shoes, a hat, glasses or a ring; 'take off' is خَلَعَ.

examples.note: he put on a shirt / shoes / glasses

model.other: ar:labisa (cr.01) has the senses verb.getdressed, verb.puton and verb.wear.

phenomena.gap: خَلَعَ “to take off” is not a lexeme yet; the garments come in the clothes lesson (cr.08).

phenomena.title: One general 'carry'
phenomena.what: حَمَلَ 'carry' covers carrying in the hands, in the arms, on the back or on the head; the manner is added only when needed.

examples.note: he carried the bag on his back

phenomena.gap: حَمَلَ is not a lexeme yet.

phenomena.title: One general 'cut'
phenomena.what: قَطَعَ 'cut' is the default for any cutting; more specific verbs exist (قَصَّ with scissors, ذَبَحَ slaughter, حَلَقَ shave) but are not required.
phenomena.gap: قَطَعَ is not a lexeme yet.

phenomena.title: Green and blue are two colours
phenomena.what: أَخْضَرُ 'green' and أَزْرَقُ 'blue' are separate basic colour words, both of the colour pattern أَفْعَل / فَعْلَاء / فُعْل.

phenomena.title: Direction in the verb, manner added
phenomena.what: The direction of movement is in the verb (دَخَلَ go in, خَرَجَ go out, صَعِدَ go up, نَزَلَ go down, عَبَرَ cross, رَجَعَ come back); the manner, if said, is added as a ḥāl or a phrase.
phenomena.gap: دَخَلَ / خَرَجَ are taught (fd.13); صَعِدَ, نَزَلَ, عَبَرَ are not lexemes, and adding the manner as a ḥāl is not taught.

phenomena.title: Location without posture verbs
phenomena.what: Where something is located is said without a verb of posture: the nominal sentence (or كَانَ / يُوجَدُ when a verb is needed) is used for anything, lying, standing or hanging. جَلَسَ 'sit', وَقَفَ 'stand', اِسْتَلْقَى 'lie' describe what bodies do.

examples.note: the book is on the table
the picture is (hangs) on the wall

phenomena.title: Large numbers by thousands
